The paper proposes a new IRS-aided electromagnetic stealth system mounted on moving targets to evade detection from distributed radars.
The IRS is composed of N = N_x × N_y passive reflecting elements, each of which can be digitally controlled to induce an independent amplitude change and/or phase shift.
For the single-radar case, the authors derive a semi-closed-form optimal solution for the IRS's reflection optimization problem using the Lagrange multiplier method.
For the multi-radar case, the IRS's reflection optimization problem is formulated as a convex QCQP and solved optimally.
The paper proposes low-complexity closed-form solutions based on the reverse alignment and minimum mean-square error (MMSE) criteria for the single-radar and multi-radar cases, respectively.
To acquire the necessary angle-of-arrival and/or path gain information, the authors develop practical low-complexity estimation schemes at the target for both single-radar and multi-radar setups.

Simulation results show that the proposed IRS-aided electromagnetic stealth system significantly reduces and even eliminates the signal reflected by the target, achieving satisfactory stealth performance.
The effect of imperfect angle-of-arrival information at the target on the radar performance is also investigated in the paper.
Existing electromagnetic stealth materials/metasurfaces lack flexibility and adaptability, and can only operate within a limited frequency and angle/direction range.

The high mobility of the target and rapid operational radar mode changes can result in quick alterations in detection frequency and incident wave angles, rendering traditional electromagnetic stealth materials inapplicable.
